transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Lin (Redwood AE); Carlos Mendez (Redwood SE); Aisha Rahman (Coastline Platform Eng); Tom Berger (Coastline ML Eng); Lena Park (Coastline SRE)

Summary:
Weekly POC check-in focused on throughput/latency tradeoffs, continuous batching tuning, concurrency targets, and queue-shaping for smoother burst behavior. Agreed to run a short controlled loadtest on Dedicated staging and to share traces and sim results next week. Action items and dates captured.

Topics: flow conditioning, continuous batching, concurrency caps, backpressure smoothing, KV cache effects, burst capacity pricing, p95/p99 latency buckets.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: hey everyone thanks for joining, um, quick roll call and then we'll jump into the head lines. Sofia? sorry I mean Sophie, that's me. Carlos, take it away for the health checks?
[00:18] Carlos: yeah sure, real quick. We've been running the continuous batching config you asked for last week, set the batching windows to adaptive 10-150ms and the queue depth cap at 64. Observed avg token throughput up about 15%, cost per token down roughly 12% in these runs, but p95 latency bumped to about 420 ms in the mid-burst.
[00:42] Aisha: right so the 420 p95 is what we saw in our internal spikes as well, that still is a bit high for our user-facing SLO which is 300 p95. We're hoping to get that under 300 while keeping costs within the pilot cap.
[01:05] Carlos: yeah totally. There's a tradeoff. If we lower batching window we reduce p95 but throughput drops. We can instead target concurrency shaping plus queue smoothing so bursts don't push batch build times up.
[01:28] Tom: can you unpack "queue smoothing" a little? we've been thinking in terms of a simple FIFO queue and a hard concurrency cap.
[01:40] Carlos: sure. So two pieces: one, dynamic concurrency target that ramps with observed latency buckets — slow ramp up on sudden spikes — and two, a small reservoir queue with prioritized prefix hits for KV cache to avoid rebuilding KV for repeated contexts. Implemented as a shape function we call flow conditioning here. It's not perfect, um, and the current transcription of the model's KV cache is... the logs show some evictions under 3k sequence churn.
[02:08] Lena: eviction sounds familiar. Our SRE team saw something similar where the KV cash — cash, sorry, I mean cache — was thrashing at high concurrency and sequence variance. Is there an easy knob for retention?
[02:22] Carlos: yeah retention TTLs and batch affinity help. We can pin longer TTL for session tokens and set batch affinity so requests from the same user are steered to the same worker for a short window. That reduces cache misses and lowers tail latency.
[02:39] Sophie: quick clarifying question for Coastline — what's acceptable for p95 vs p99? are you chasing 300ms p95 only or p99 also?
[02:49] Aisha: primary is p95 300ms. p99 we'd like under 800ms but it's less strict. If p95 is good we're happy to accept p99 variance as long as it doesn't spike to multiple seconds.
[03:02] Sophie: good. OK that gives us measurable targets. Carlos, can you propose concurrency targets for steady-state vs spikes?
[03:12] Carlos: initial suggestion: steady-state concurrency 8, allow burst to 20 with queue shaping to keep in-flight batches stable. For the Dedicated staging we should test 12 steady / 36 burst to see headroom. The important thing is stair-step ramp, not immediate jump.
[03:32] Tom: 36 burst seems high — what's the expected per-GPU throughput at that setting? I assume model is 7B quantized?
[03:38] Carlos: yeah 7B q4, roughly 280-320 tokens/s per GPU at the current kernel mix with continuous batching. With concurrency 36 we saturate and queue latency climbs so we need the shaping to stagger requests, otherwise p95 blows out.
[03:56] Aisha: can we also test changing the initial batching window floor to 6ms? we tried 10-150 last run.
[04:05] Carlos: yep we can try 6-120 and also a mid-window of ~30ms as default. Might lower p95 a bit but cost per token might rise. We'll put both in the sim.
[04:18] Sophie: quick question about metrics — what dashboards do you want us to produce? token-level cost, p50/p95/p99, KV cache hit rate, batch size distribution?
[04:29] Lena: yes all of those. Also include task queue depth histogram and worker utilization. Our SRE wants to see per-node memory pressure when KV cache retention is increased.
[04:40] Carlos: got it. We'll add a per-worker mem + KV hits chart.
[04:44] [05:02] Speaker 1: (inaudible) sorry.
[05:15] Tom: one thing we ran into — when we tried affinity steering a few days ago requests got unevenly spread and some workers idled while others had big batches. Any tips on preventing hot spots?
[05:29] Carlos: yes, that's where fair hashing + small sticky window helps. Don't make affinity permanent; keep it in the order of seconds so it helps KV without causing long-lived hot spots. Also queue-weighted routing to less busy workers can help smooth load.
[05:47] Aisha: for the KV TTL, is there a recommended default? we don't want to blow memory.
[05:54] Carlos: in our experience 30s to 2m depending on session churn. Start with 45s for your workload and monitor mem pressure.
[06:05] Sophie: ok let's talk about the Controlled loadtest we agreed to do in staging. Plan?
[06:11] Lena: we can provision a temporary Dedicated staging spot with the same GPU type as production. We'll peer VPCs and run a 2 hour run next Tuesday, start at low rps, ramp to target 400 rps then apply burst pattern.
[06:24] Tom: can we capture raw request traces during that run? we can send them back to you for deeper analysis.
[06:29] Sophie: yes please, anonymized traces are perfect — we can plug them into the sim and calibrate the shaping function.
[06:35] Aisha: shipping traces will need an internal redaction step. We'll do that and share by Monday.
[06:41] Sophie: great. On pricing, the customer asked about burst capacity cost — I'll send an updated sheet showing per-hour burst increments and cost/benefit analysis.
[06:50] Aisha: yes please include an example: 2 hour sustained burst vs short spikes, and the fallback model variant pricing if we drop to a cheaper 3B for overflow.
[06:59] Carlos: small note on fallback models — switching to a smaller model reduces latency but also reduces quality and might change token counts; we should measure end-to-end user impact.
[07:12] Tom: agreed. We might prefer partial responses or progressive decode strategies rather than switching models.
[07:20] Sophie: ok moving on, quick review of last week's sim results — Carlos?
[07:24] Carlos: last week's sim (attached link) ran three scenarios: baseline FIFO with hard cap, adaptive batching with fixed concurrency, and adaptive batching + flow conditioning. Baseline p95 was 610ms, adaptive batching got to 420ms but had cost savings. Flow conditioning reduced p95 to ~320ms and improved 95th tail stability, with about 8% cost overhead vs pure adaptive batching.
[07:50] Aisha: that's promising. The 320 p95 is close to our target. Is the extra 8% acceptable? we'll check with finance but sounds doable if it prevents user-visible errors.
[07:59] Sophie: another follow-up — what was KV hit rate difference between the runs?
[08:03] Carlos: baseline KV hit ~18%, adaptive ~27%, flow conditioning ~46% in the sim because affinity + TTL reduced misses. That correlated strongly with better p95.
[08:16] Lena: nice. Anything else in the sim we should watch for?
[08:21] Carlos: memory pressure spikes on workers when TTL increased — we saw 12% higher mem usage during peak. We'll include safe TTL recommendations.
[08:31] Aisha: is there any chance we could leverage Redwood's built-in prefix caching for some static prompts to reduce re-eval cost?
[08:39] Carlos: yes, prefix caching for templates works well; we'll propose which prompts from your sample traces are good candidates.
[08:46] Tom: about the fallback model — can Redwood do automatic fallback at the routing layer when Dedicated is saturated?
[08:53] Sophie: yes we support automated fallbacks to a cheaper model variant or to a hosted pool. You can configure policies like latency-first or cost-first. We'll send a sample policy YAML.
[09:05] Aisha: we want fail-open behavior where critical flows go to the hosted premium lane if Dedicated is saturated. non-critical flows can be queued or served with the 3B variant.
[09:16] Carlos: okay we'll draft a routing policy for that.
[09:19] [09:45] Speaker 2: (background noise)
[09:52] Sophie: quick admin — Sophie to send pricing; Carlos to run sims with 6ms-120ms batching window and a 12/36 staging config; Aisha to share traces; Lena to provision peer.
[10:06] Tom: can we also get a small sample Jupyter that runs the sim locally so we can tweak parameters ourselves?
[10:12] Carlos: yes we have a small sim notebook, we'll share a sanitized version you can run against redwood-sim data.
[10:18] Aisha: good. Also please include instructions on how to interpret the batch size distribution chart — we had some confusion last time about the mean vs median.
[10:27] Carlos: will do; we'll add a legend and notes.
[10:31] Sophie: anything else from the customer side?
[10:33] Lena: just one SRE ask — include a short runbook for if the KV cache starts thrashing during a release window. Our ops folks want concrete rollback steps.
[10:40] Carlos: we can provide a runbook snippet: drop TTL, disable affinity, reduce concurrency, and optionally divert to hosted lane. We'll submit that as a short doc.
[10:50] Aisha: thanks.
[10:53] Sophie: ok wrapping up, recap of next steps and owners... (recap follows)
[11:04] Sophie: Carlos, anything you'd add?
[11:08] Carlos: just that we should consider a small A/B in production later: half users mild shaping, half no shaping, measure retention/engagement. But that's for after the pilot.
[11:19] Aisha: agreed. Let's do the staging runs first.
[11:22] Sophie: perfect, we'll reconvene next Tuesday same time to go over sim results and staging run outcomes. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
